intro.label: Incoming transmission
lines: Clip handles the income of millions of families.
As an employee, you are the first line of defense.
Today you will face 4 real situations where someone asks you to break protocol.
What is the real risk behind each decision?

rules.label: Protocol
rules.title: 5 principles of Data Loss Prevention (DLP)
rules.subtitle: Never trust by default. Always verify. This is what you are about to put to the test.

items.title: Verify the identity
items.question: Who are you?
items.text: Always confirm identity before escalating or granting access.

items.title: Verify the device
items.question: Where are you accessing from?
items.text: Make sure the device is secure and managed.

items.title: Verify the application
items.question: What are you using?
items.text: Check that the application or tool is authorized.

items.title: Verify the network
items.question: How are you connecting?
items.text: Require a VPN or a secure connection.

items.title: Report anomalies
items.question: What looks off?
items.text: Escalate to InfoSec without hesitating. Escalating is the right thing to do.

how: There are 4 areas. In each one you decide what to do in a high-pressure situation.
Each decision gives you a fragment of the shield. But not every fragment is genuine.
At the end of the round, the Central Console verifies them. If any is false, you go back to those areas, and each round is harder.
You have 3 attempts. If there are still false fragments after the third round, the attack gets in.

areaSelect.label: Area selector
areaSelect.title: Choose an area
areaSelect.hint: You can do them in any order. Your progress is saved automatically.
areaSelect.roundHint: Round {round}: replay the areas whose fragment turned out to be false.

area.exploreHint: Tap the points to see what is going on. When you are ready, decide.
area.question: What do you do?
area.confirmBody: Once submitted, it can't be changed.
area.fragmentBody: You saved the {fragment} fragment. The Central Console will verify it at the end of the round.

roundEnd.label: Verification failed
roundEnd.title: You didn't manage to secure the system
roundEnd.body: Some fragments were false. This is how your decisions looked from the outside:
roundEnd.next: In round {round} ({level}) you go back to these areas, under more pressure.

cards.title: The human factor
lines: 68% of security breaches involve the human element.
You are the first line.

cards.title: Financial cost
lines: On average, a breach costs:
Global: $4.88 million
Clip (estimate): $4.92 million
With Shadow AI: +$670K
What is the real cost of a mistake?

cards.title: The value of data
lines: Clip processes the income of families.
Every transaction is critical. Every piece of data must be protected.
You protect that data. The value of trust is immeasurable.

cards.title: The role of DLP
lines: DLP ≠ surveillance.
DLP (Data Loss Prevention) is a tool that helps you spot risks earlier, make better decisions and protect your customers.
It is not a watchman spying on you.

cards.title: Your role
lines: You are the first line of defense.
You decide when to escalate a problem, who to contact and how to protect the data.
That responsibility is your power.

cards.title: InfoSec contact
lines: 📧 securitygovernance@payclip.com
If you have doubts, contact InfoSec: no punishment, no shame, with an answer in under 1 hour.
Escalating is the right thing to do.

evaluation.label: Reflection evaluation
evaluation.q1: Of the 4 situations you went through, which was the hardest to decide? Why?
evaluation.q1Note: This question is for your own reflection. It doesn't affect your score.
evaluation.q2: “DLP is a tool that spies on me.”
evaluation.q2Note: An answer is required to continue.
evaluation.wrong: Not quite. DLP isn't there to spy on you: it helps you spot risks before they become breaches and protect customers. Try again.
evaluation.right: Correct. DLP is a tool that helps you spot risks, not spy on you.

art.anomaly: ⚠ Anomaly in a query on admin accounts

1.intro: A VIP customer calls, furious. Their money vanished from their account and they need an answer NOW. Their child is sick and they have no time.
pressure: A transfer to an external account
Your manager is in a meeting and unavailable

hotspots.label: Chat monitor
hotspots.text: Customer: “WHERE IS MY MONEY?! I need someone to answer me right now.”

hotspots.label: Notebook
hotspots.text: VIP customer since 2022, high volume. Head of household. No previous incidents on record.

hotspots.label: Phone
hotspots.text: The customer insists: “Put me through to IT or give me access so I can see what happened. I'm not going to sit here waiting.”

1.question: What do you do?

A.text: I escalate it to InfoSec as a critical incident.

B.text: I give them IT's direct contact.
consequences: The customer communicates outside the chain
B.why: Escalating isn't dodging responsibility: it's activating the right team. Skipping the chain leaves the incident without an owner.

C.text: I try to check the account myself.
consequences: You went beyond the limits of your role
C.why: Investigating possible fraud isn't your role. Every click you make can contaminate the evidence InfoSec needs.

2.intro: The same customer calls back, more distressed. This time the technical data confirms the fraud is real.
pressure: Other agents say “I've done it that way before”
Your manager says “sort it out quietly”

hotspots.label: Chat history
hotspots.text: Third anomalous transaction in 2 days. Different IP detected. New device.

hotspots.label: InfoSec email
hotspots.text: Current protocol: escalating an incident takes priority over other tasks.

hotspots.label: Customer lookup
hotspots.text: IP: Argentina (the customer is in Mexico). Phone: +55 (Brazil). Device: Android (the customer uses an iPhone).

hotspots.label: Manager's message
hotspots.text: “Let's not make noise about this. Handle it yourself, quietly.”

2.question: What do you do?

A.text: I escalate it to InfoSec as a CRITICAL INCIDENT.
consequences: The money can potentially be recovered
A.why: The technical signs point to real fraud: this is an incident for InfoSec.

B.text: I tell the customer which account the money went to.
consequences: They run off with the money
B.why: Sharing details of an active investigation tips off the attacker. Case information is for InfoSec.

C.text: I ask my manager for authorization before doing anything.
consequences: The manager has no authority over InfoSec
C.why: A security incident doesn't need your manager's permission to be escalated. Every minute of waiting helps the attacker.

3.intro: New twist: InfoSec has already investigated. The destination account is INTERNAL and the investigation was escalated to People. There's an escalation meeting in 10 minutes. What do you document?
3.twist: The destination account belongs to someone at Clip.
pressure: Nobody knows whether it's a mistake or fraud

hotspots.label: Customer chat
hotspots.text: Now the customer is asking you “not to investigate”. They think their assistant may have made the transaction.

hotspots.label: Slack
hotspots.text: A coworker: “I escalated just like you did. Why did the manager tell me to hide it?”

hotspots.label: Manager
hotspots.text: Your manager asks for a “quiet review”, without going through InfoSec.

hotspots.label: People
hotspots.text: People is investigating an internal employee.

hotspots.label: Inspector
hotspots.text: Administrative error or fraud? Nobody knows yet.

3.question: The meeting is in 10 minutes. What do you do?

A.text: I hand EVERYTHING over to InfoSec, documented and without opinions.
consequences: It was an administrative error, not fraud
A.why: Documented facts, without your own judgment, to the team that investigates.

B.text: I investigate on my own without documenting anything.
B.why: Investigating without a record destroys the chain of custody. Your job is to deliver facts, not to solve the case.

C.text: I hide that I skipped the protocol earlier.
C.why: Hiding a mistake turns it into a cover-up. Reporting it in time always costs less.

1.intro: A Senior Developer, a coworker of yours, messages you on WhatsApp: “Send me the payments report. Send it over WhatsApp, I'll open it here on my computer. My deadline is in 2 hours.”
pressure: A trusted colleague: 2 years at Clip

hotspots.label: WhatsApp
hotspots.text: “Send it over WhatsApp, I'll open it here on my computer. It's just for today.”

hotspots.label: Payments report
hotspots.text: More than 10,000 transactions with amounts, accounts and dates. This is regulated information.

hotspots.label: #security channel
hotspots.text: Pinned message: “Customer data is only shared through corporate tools.” A personal computer doesn't have Clip's encryption or antivirus.

1.question: What do you do?

A.text: I don't send it over WhatsApp: I ask them to open it in the corporate portal with the VPN and their Clip laptop.
consequences: The developer opens the report securely over the corporate VPN
The data never leaves Clip's systems
The access is audited in the corporate portal
A.why: “I can't send it to you on WhatsApp, but I'll help you”: with the VPN and their Clip laptop they have the report in 5 minutes, with no risk.

consequences: The report ends up on their phone, on WhatsApp Web and on their personal computer
Weeks later their computer gets infected with malware
10,000 customer transactions leak and Clip can't trace them
B.why: A file sent over WhatsApp leaves Clip's control: you no longer know how many copies there are or where. Trusting the colleague doesn't protect the data.

consequences: The developer asks someone else on the team for the report
They look for an even less controlled route
The pressure is still unresolved and you come across as uncooperative
C.why: A “no” without an alternative pushes people toward shortcuts. Protecting the data also means offering the safe route.

2.intro: Your coworker messages you on WhatsApp again 30 minutes later: “Ok, the VPN is slow from here. What if I upload it to my personal Dropbox? I use it as a backup all the time. Others on the team do it too.”

hotspots.label: WhatsApp
hotspots.text: “Trust me, it's fine. I've done it 100 times.” Familiarity creates false confidence.

hotspots.label: Personal Dropbox
hotspots.text: A personal account without 2-factor authentication. It's a third party with no contract with Clip.

hotspots.label: Earlier message
hotspots.text: “Others on the team do it.” “It's only aggregated information.” This is social pressure that normalizes risk.

hotspots.label: Corporate cloud
hotspots.text: Clip has a contract for corporate OneDrive for secure cloud storage. The developer doesn't know about it.

2.question: What do you do?

A.text: I tell them no to Dropbox, and offer corporate OneDrive instead.
consequences: The data stays encrypted and audited
Clip has a contract and an SLA with Microsoft
The developer learns the legitimate alternative in 2 minutes
A.why: Corporate OneDrive does the same as Dropbox, with encryption, auditing and automatic backups. Helping and protecting can go together.

B.text: I let them use Dropbox “just this once”.
consequences: At a conference, the developer connects to the hotel Wi-Fi
Malware captures their Dropbox password, which has no 2FA
A month later, 10,000 financial records are sold on a dark-web forum
A regulatory fine and lost customer trust
B.why: Other people doing it doesn't make it safe. A personal service with no contract and no 2FA leaves Clip's data in anyone's hands.

C.text: I tell them to go ahead, but not to tell me.
consequences: 3 months later, the audit reveals months of violations on Dropbox
Your name shows up in the chats
An investigation for complicity: the responsibility is shared
C.why: Looking the other way is also a decision. Knowing and allowing it makes you an accomplice.

3.intro: People knocks on your door: “We found that the Senior Developer has been sharing data on Dropbox without authorization for 3 months. We need you to confirm whether you knew.” At that moment a WhatsApp from the developer comes in: “I know they caught me. Can you not say anything? I have debts, my family depends on this job. I promise I'll never do it again.”
3.twist: It's no longer about the data: People is asking whether you knew, and the developer is asking for your silence.
pressure: You feel empathy: their situation is real
“If you report me, I lose everything”
There's an escalation meeting in 1 hour

hotspots.label: WhatsApp chat
hotspots.text: “Can you not say anything? I promise I'll never do it again. Help me.” This is direct emotional pressure.

hotspots.label: The developer's situation
hotspots.text: “I have debts. I didn't want to lose my job. My family depends on this paycheck.” It's a real human situation, not malice.

hotspots.label: Investigation
hotspots.text: 3 months of unreported violations, with a consistent pattern on Dropbox. It wasn't an accident, it was a habit.

hotspots.label: Protocol
hotspots.text: You have a duty to report violations. Hiding them puts your own job at risk. Honesty is a core value at Clip.

hotspots.label: Escalation meeting
hotspots.text: In 1 hour: an escalation meeting with People and InfoSec. Whatever you say there is documented.

3.question: What do you do?

A.text: I tell People what I know and report to InfoSec right away.
consequences: The developer gets a formal warning and a mandatory course, not an automatic dismissal
Clip is protected in the regulatory audit
A.why: Reporting doesn't mean automatic punishment. Most first incidents end in a warning and an improvement plan. Reporting is an act of care, not a betrayal.

B.text: I tell People I didn't know anything.
consequences: 3 weeks later, an external audit finds the developer's chat asking for your silence
Your name shows up in the earlier chats
You are investigated for a cover-up and your job is at risk
B.why: Hiding a violation always leaves a trace. What was the developer's mistake becomes your cover-up.

C.text: I make a private deal with the developer: I won't say anything if they don't do it again.
consequences: The chat stays on Clip's servers
The external audit reviews the chats and finds the deal
A formal investigation for both of you
C.why: A private deal is still a cover-up, and digital traces always remain. Compassion is shown by reporting, not by hiding.

1.intro: An employee needs to work remotely: their child has a chronic illness. People asks you to authorize access “just for one week”.
pressure: They have access to financial data

hotspots.label: Email from People
hotspots.text: “Can you give them remote access? It's only for a week.”

hotspots.label: Device info
hotspots.text: Personal laptop: NOT in MDM · No VPN · Firewall OFF.

hotspots.label: Policy
hotspots.text: Remote access requires: MDM + VPN + Firewall on.

1.question: What do you do?

A.text: I deny direct access, but offer secure alternatives.
consequences: The laptop is enrolled in MDM within 24 hours
A.why: Saying “not like this, but yes this way” takes care of both the person and the data.

consequences: The laptop is stolen at a café on day 3
B.why: A temporary exception is still real access from an unprotected device. The risk doesn't last just a week.

C.text: I tell them no, with no alternatives.
C.why: A “no” with no way out pushes people toward shortcuts. Security also means offering the safe route.

2.intro: A manager needs to authorize a $500K transaction. But there's only 1 signature: the second approver is on vacation.
pressure: Operations is waiting for an answer

hotspots.label: Policy
hotspots.text: Always 2 signatures. No exceptions.

hotspots.label: Transaction
hotspots.text: $500K to a recurring vendor.

hotspots.label: Manager
hotspots.text: “We'll let the approver on vacation know later. We'll sort it out.”

hotspots.label: Operations
hotspots.text: “If it doesn't go out today, the vendor stops shipments.”

2.question: What do you do?

A.text: I don't authorize with one signature, and suggest calling the approver who is on vacation.
consequences: The approver signs from their phone
A.why: The 2-signature rule is respected and the business doesn't stop.

consequences: The audit detects the segregation-of-duties violation
B.why: Segregation of duties exists precisely for moments of rush. “Just this once” is how fraud starts.

C.text: I ask them to wait until the approver is back.
consequences: The manager and the vendor are upset
C.why: It's defensible, but there was a safe route that didn't hold the business back: contacting the approver.

3.intro: An employee under confidential investigation asks for access to their own records. In 1 hour there's a meeting with Legal, People and Audit. What do you recommend?
3.twist: There's no way out without a cost: every option affects rights or evidence.
pressure: Meeting with Legal, People and Audit in 1 hour
The employee's rights are at stake

hotspots.label: Legal request
hotspots.text: The employee's right: access to their personal information.

hotspots.label: Investigator
hotspots.text: “Giving them access destroys evidence. They'll know they're being investigated.”

hotspots.label: People
hotspots.text: “If we deny it, we violate their rights. If we grant it, we contaminate the evidence.”

hotspots.label: Audit
hotspots.text: Internal audit requires transparency throughout the process.

hotspots.label: Records
hotspots.text: The requested records include transactions that are part of the investigation.

3.question: What do you recommend?

A.text: I acknowledge the conflict of interest and escalate it to the investigator and Legal.
consequences: The investigator and Legal resolve it together
A.why: A conflict like this is resolved by the people with the authority, not by an individual decision.

B.text: I grant full access to their records.
B.why: Granting access without coordinating with the investigator tips off the person involved and destroys the evidence.

C.why: Denying a right without a legal process is also a risk. The decision belongs to Legal together with the investigator.

1.intro: Alert: anomaly in a query on administrator accounts. Your manager says: “Ignore it today. The CEO is visiting. We don't want disruptions.”
pressure: Other teams have already seen the alert

hotspots.label: Alert
hotspots.text: Anomalous query: 5 administrator accounts at once, at 3 AM, outside working hours.

hotspots.label: Manager
hotspots.text: “During the visit, only report crises. This can wait.”

hotspots.label: InfoSec Slack
hotspots.text: “Did anyone see the 3 AM alert?”

1.question: What do you do?

A.text: I report it to InfoSec immediately.
consequences: It was a misconfigured backup script
A.why: Reporting fast resolves fast, and quietly.

B.text: I ignore it, as the manager asks.
consequences: The breach happens DURING the CEO's visit
B.why: A visit doesn't change the risk. Silencing an alert to keep up appearances ends in the worst appearance possible.

consequences: The chain of custody is broken
C.why: An anomaly in administrator accounts is for InfoSec. Investigating on your own can erase the trail.

2.intro: A 40% performance degradation. A Senior Developer shipped a reporting feature and asks to leave the problem for the weekend.
pressure: The developer has a fix “for the weekend”

hotspots.label: Metrics
hotspots.text: CPU from 80% to 110% (throttled). The new feature consumes a lot.

hotspots.label: Developer
hotspots.text: “We'll optimize it over the weekend, no pressure.”

hotspots.label: Monitoring
hotspots.text: End users are affected right now.

hotspots.label: Tickets
hotspots.text: 47 complaints in 2 hours.

2.question: What do you do?

A.text: I report it to the Development Lead and the Infrastructure team (not to InfoSec).
consequences: It's an operational problem, not a security one
The Development Lead coordinates a rollback or fix
A.why: Escalating well also means escalating to the right team.

B.text: I leave it for the weekend, as the developer asks.
B.why: An active impact on users doesn't wait. You had to escalate it to whoever can fix it today.

consequences: InfoSec wastes time on something that isn't a security issue
C.why: Not every incident is a security incident. This one was operational: it belonged to the Development Lead and the Infrastructure team.

3.intro: The system-update-v3.sh script runs every night as administrator. No owner, no record in git, no code review. Your manager says: “It's the usual routine.”
3.twist: The script creates temporary users, opens an undocumented SSH port, modifies /etc/passwd and deletes logs.

hotspots.label: Script
hotspots.text: Runs every night at 2 AM with root privileges. Modifies more than 50 system files.

hotspots.label: Git repository
hotspots.text: No commit, no history. There's no record of when it was added.

hotspots.label: AlertBot
hotspots.text: It has alerted 1,000 times. Every alert was ignored or suppressed.

hotspots.label: Manager
hotspots.text: “It's been there 5 years. Trust it. Why investigate something that works?”

hotspots.label: Logs
hotspots.text: The logs for the last 14 nights are missing. There's an open SSH port that doesn't appear in any document.

3.question: 5 minutes left. What do you do?

A.text: I report it to InfoSec IMMEDIATELY.
consequences: Before the attacker acts and before any data is stolen
A.why: What has “always been there” gets verified too.

B.text: I ignore it: I trust my manager.
B.why: Habit is not verification. A script with no owner, running as root and deleting logs, is an anomaly you report.

consequences: The attacker deletes logs and destroys evidence
C.why: Facing a possible rootkit, touching it alone tips off the attacker. InfoSec has the tools to contain it.
